newsitem.title: FRENCH POLYNESIA: French Polynesian islands seek closer Paris ties.
newsitem.headline: French Polynesian islands seek closer Paris ties.

text.p: Following the lead of unhappy residents of the Comoros island group, some dissatisfied denizens of French Polynesia are now seeking closer ties to France for their island home.

Lucien Kimitete, mayor of the South Pacific island of Nuku Hiva, urged Paris at the weekend to transform the Marquesas islands, now a part of the semi-autonomous territory of French Polynesia, into a full-fledged part of France in the form of an overseas department.

"Polynesia's autonomous status does not inspire our confidence. There is a risk, in our eyes, that the territory could become independent," Kimitete told Jean-Jack Queyranne, French visiting junior minister for overseas territories.

Queyranne thanked Kimitete for his kind words concerning France but flatly ruled out departmental status for Nuku Hiva, a part of the Marquesas island group located some 1,500 km (900 miles) northeast of the French Polynesian capital Papeete, located on the island of Tahiti.
"We cannot create an overseas department here," Queyranne later told reporters. He said he had interpreted Kimitete's statement as "a request for state recognition and support".
Support for complete independence from France is confined to a vocal minority in French Polynesia, which is heavily dependent on French financial support.
Departmental status for the Marquesas would mean significantly more aid for the island group.
Two of the three Indian Ocean islands making up the Islamic Republic of Comoros have in recent weeks declared their independence from the Republic and asked to return to French rule.

Separatists on the islands of Anjouan and Moheli argue they have experienced nothing but poverty and political unrest since the archipelago gained its independence from France in 1975, in contrast to the comparative prosperity on the nearby island of Mayotte, which voted against independence and remains under French rule.
France has refused to back the revolt, saying this would constitute interference in the republic's internal affairs.

The demands for closer ties have embarrassed France at a time when it is trying to take a lower profile in its former colonies, announcing plans to withdraw troops from Africa and limiting future military interventions.
